title: OB, Pediatrics & Geriatrics
summary: Pregnancy emergencies, delivering a baby, resuscitating a newborn, sizing up a sick child, and the traps that come with very old patients and patients with special needs.

lessons.title: Pregnancy changes the rules
lessons.body:
Every pregnant patient is two patients, and the one you cannot see gets shortchanged first. Almost every rule below comes from that single fact.

## More blood means hidden shock

By the third trimester a pregnant patient carries about `50%` more blood volume than before pregnancy — an extra `1 to 1.5 liters`. Her resting heart rate runs about `10 to 15` beats per minute faster, and her blood pressure sits `5 to 15 mmHg` lower in the second trimester before drifting back up.

That extra volume is a buffer, and the body spends it strategically. When she bleeds, the uterus is the first vascular bed clamped down so the brain and heart keep their supply. She can lose `1,500 mL` — roughly a third of her volume — and still hold a nearly normal blood pressure.

> **Key:** In pregnancy, normal vital signs do not rule out shock. Act on the mechanism, the estimated blood loss, the skin signs and the heart rate — not on a reassuring blood pressure.

By the time her pressure finally drops she has lost `30 to 35%` of her volume, and the fetus has been under-perfused for a while. Oxygen, positioning, warmth and rapid transport start on suspicion.

## The vein under the uterus

After about `20 weeks` — roughly when the top of the uterus (the fundus) reaches the belly button — the uterus is heavy enough that lying flat drops it onto the inferior vena cava, the large vein returning blood from the legs to the heart. Less blood comes back, so less goes out: pressure falls and she turns pale, sweaty, nauseated and lightheaded. That is **supine hypotensive syndrome**.

The fix is free and immediate. Tilt her `15 to 30 degrees` onto her **left** side. If she is strapped to a long board, tilt the whole board and pad under the right hip. If she has to stay flat for CPR, push the uterus up and toward her left with your gloved hands (manual uterine displacement).

> **On shift:** A pregnant patient who suddenly goes pale the second you lay her on the stretcher is usually not deteriorating — she is on her back. Tilt her left and watch her color return in about `30 seconds`.

## A stomach that does not empty

Pregnancy hormones relax the valve at the top of the stomach, and the pregnant stomach empties more slowly, so food sits there long after a meal. Add a uterus pushing upward on everything and the pressure inside the abdomen is high. The result is a much higher **aspiration risk** — stomach contents spilling into the lungs.

Practically: have suction on and within reach, ventilate gently with just enough volume to raise the chest so you do not force air into the stomach, and if she is unresponsive be ready to log-roll and suction fast.

## Breathing, and trauma

The uterus shoves the diaphragm up, so she takes smaller breaths more often and her oxygen reserve is small — saturation falls quickly when ventilation stops. A respiratory rate over `24` is abnormal.

For trauma, the whole approach collapses into one sentence: treat the mother. High-flow oxygen, control bleeding, keep her warm, tilt left, transport to a trauma center. Even a low-speed crash can shear the placenta off the uterine wall, so any pregnant trauma patient past `20 weeks` gets evaluated at the hospital, however good she looks.

> **Trap:** 'Treat the fetus' is never the answer on the exam. The best fetal care is a warm, oxygenated, well-perfused, left-tilted mother.
keyPoints: Blood volume rises about 50%, so shock shows up late — normal vitals do not mean stable.
After 20 weeks, lying flat compresses the vena cava: tilt 15 to 30 degrees left or manually displace the uterus.
Delayed gastric emptying plus a crowded abdomen means high aspiration risk — suction ready, ventilate gently.
Resting HR runs 10 to 15 beats faster and BP a little lower; RR over 24 is abnormal.
In trauma, treat the mother: oxygen, bleeding control, left tilt, rapid transport.

checks.q: A 33-week pregnant patient is placed flat on the stretcher and within a minute becomes pale, sweaty and lightheaded with a BP of 86/50. What do you do first?
choices: Tilt her 15 to 30 degrees onto her left side
Sit her fully upright
Raise both legs 12 inches while she stays flat
Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
checks.why: This is supine hypotensive syndrome: the uterus is compressing the vena cava. Left tilt restores venous return instantly. Leg elevation does not fix the obstruction, and she is breathing on her own.

checks.q: A 28-week pregnant patient has lost an estimated 1,200 mL of blood. Her BP is 116/70 and her heart rate is 108. What does that tell you?
choices: She is stable because her blood pressure is normal
She is in shock and the normal BP is expected because of increased blood volume
The blood loss estimate must be wrong
She has lost less than 10% of her blood volume
checks.why: Extra blood volume plus shunting away from the uterus keeps the pressure up until about a third of volume is gone. The tachycardia is the early sign; treat for shock.

checks.q: Why is a pregnant patient at higher risk of aspiration?
choices: Her cough reflex disappears in the third trimester
Her tidal volume doubles
The stomach empties more slowly and the valve above it relaxes
Pregnancy causes excess saliva production
checks.why: Hormonal relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter plus delayed gastric emptying and upward pressure from the uterus means a full stomach under pressure. Have suction ready and ventilate gently.

lessons.title: OB emergencies: bleeding, pain and seizures
lessons.body:
Four pictures cover most of what will kill a pregnant patient before the hospital: a pregnancy in the wrong place, a placenta in the wrong place, a placenta that tore loose, and a blood pressure that got out of control.

## Ectopic pregnancy

A fertilized egg implants outside the uterus, almost always in a fallopian tube. The tube is not built to stretch, so around `6 to 8 weeks` it ruptures and bleeds into the abdomen. This is the leading cause of death in the first trimester.

The classic triad is a **missed period**, **one-sided lower abdominal pain**, and **vaginal bleeding** — but the bleeding is often light or absent, because the blood is pouring into the belly, not out. Blood on the diaphragm irritates a nerve that also serves the shoulder, so referred **shoulder pain** in a woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain is a red flag.

> **Key:** Any woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain is a possible ectopic until proven otherwise — including one who says she cannot be pregnant. Treat for shock, oxygen, keep her warm, transport fast.

## Placenta previa versus abruptio placentae

Both present as third-trimester bleeding. The distinction is pain.

| | Placenta previa | Abruptio placentae |
|---|---|---|
| Problem | Placenta covers the cervix | Placenta tears off the uterine wall |
| Bleeding | Bright red, **painless**, often sudden | Dark red, **painful**, sometimes hidden |
| Uterus | Soft, normal | Rigid, board-like, tender |
| Trigger | Often spontaneous | Trauma, hypertension, cocaine |

Abruption is the more dangerous one because the bleeding can be entirely concealed behind the placenta. A pregnant patient after a crash with severe constant abdominal pain and a hard uterus is bleeding even if you see nothing.

For either one: nothing goes in the vagina, ever. No packing, no internal exam. Place pads to estimate loss, count them, give high-flow oxygen, keep her warm, left tilt, transport.

## Preeclampsia and eclampsia

After `20 weeks`, some patients develop a whole-body blood vessel problem called **preeclampsia**: blood pressure `≥ 140/90`, protein in the urine, plus swelling of the face and hands, severe headache, vision changes (spots, blurring, flashing), upper-right abdominal pain, and hyperactive reflexes.

When it progresses to a seizure, it is **eclampsia** — and it can happen up to `6 weeks` after delivery.

Management is deliberately boring: protect her from injury, do not restrain, left lateral position, suction, high-flow oxygen after the seizure, and keep the environment **dim and quiet** because light, noise and jostling can trigger another seizure. Turn off the lights bar and the siren if it is safe to do so. This patient needs an obstetric hospital and a definitive treatment (magnesium) you do not carry.

> **On the exam:** A pregnant patient over 20 weeks with a headache, blurry vision and a BP of `168/104` is a preeclampsia question. The right answer is transport in the left lateral position with minimal stimulation — not aspirin, not nitroglycerin, not a cold pack.

## Trauma in pregnancy

The uterus is a large, blood-filled organ with no protection past `20 weeks`. Even minor mechanisms cause abruption. Seatbelts should be worn low across the hips with the shoulder strap between the breasts — but a properly worn seatbelt never means she can stay home.

Every pregnant trauma patient: high-flow oxygen, control external bleeding, left tilt or board tilt, full spinal precautions if indicated, and transport to a trauma center that can perform an emergency delivery.
keyPoints: Ectopic: missed period, one-sided pain, shoulder pain, shock with little or no visible bleeding.
Previa is painless bright red bleeding; abruption is painful dark bleeding with a rigid uterus and can be concealed.
Never place anything in the vagina — pads only, count them to estimate loss.
Preeclampsia is BP 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks with headache, vision changes and edema; a seizure makes it eclampsia.
Eclampsia care: left lateral, protect, suction, oxygen, dim and quiet, rapid OB transport.

checks.q: A 34-week pregnant patient has sudden painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Her uterus is soft and non-tender. What is most likely?
choices: Abruptio placentae
Placenta previa
Uterine rupture
Ectopic pregnancy
checks.why: Painless, bright red, soft uterus is the previa pattern. Abruption hurts and makes the uterus rigid; ectopic is a first-trimester problem.

checks.q: A 30-week pregnant patient seizes at home. She stops after 90 seconds. What is your immediate priority?
choices: Place her on her left side, protect her airway, and keep the compartment dim and quiet
Restrain her arms to prevent a second seizure
Give oral glucose as soon as the seizure stops
Sit her upright and apply a blood pressure cuff before anything else
checks.why: Eclampsia care is airway, left lateral position, suction, oxygen and minimal stimulation. Restraints cause injury and stimulation can trigger another seizure.

lessons.title: Delivering a baby: the normal sequence
lessons.body:
Normal childbirth is not a medical procedure you perform. It is a process you catch, guide gently, and keep clean and warm. Your two decisions are: do I deliver here, and am I ready when the head comes.

## Deliver here, or drive?

Three findings say the baby is coming now:

1. **Crowning** — the head visible at the vaginal opening. This is the single decisive sign.
2. An overwhelming **urge to push** or a feeling of needing to have a bowel movement.
3. Contractions `2 to 3 minutes` apart lasting `60 to 90 seconds`.

Also ask: how many previous deliveries? Second and later babies come much faster. If she is crowning, you deliver where you are. If contractions are `5 or more minutes` apart and there is no crowning, transport, positioned on her left side.

> **Trap:** Driving fast with a crowning multipara is the wrong answer on the exam and in life. You will deliver a baby in a moving box with no room and no light. Stop and deliver.

## The OB kit

Sterile gloves, drapes and towels, two cord clamps, scissors or a scalpel, a bulb syringe, gauze, a plastic bag for the placenta, a baby blanket or an infant swaddler, and sanitary pads. Take the whole kit in — you cannot go back to the rig mid-delivery.

## Step by step

1. **Set up.** Gloves, gown, eye protection — delivery is a fluid event. Position her on her back with knees flexed and hips elevated a few inches on blankets, or on her side. Drape her.
2. **Control the head.** As the head crowns, place your gloved hand flat on it with gentle pressure so it comes out slowly. Fast delivery tears her tissue and can injure the baby. Do not pull, and do not press on the soft spot (fontanelle).
3. **Check for a nuchal cord.** The instant the head is out, run a finger around the neck. If the cord is there and loose, slip it gently over the head. If it is tight and cannot be slipped, clamp it in two places and cut between the clamps, then deliver immediately — the baby now has no oxygen supply.
4. **Clear the airway only if needed.** Routine suctioning is no longer recommended. Wipe the mouth and nose with gauze. If there is obstructing fluid or the baby needs ventilation, suction **mouth first, then nose**, squeezing the bulb before inserting it.
5. **Deliver the shoulders.** Support the head and guide it gently **down** to free the top shoulder, then gently **up** for the bottom shoulder. The rest slides out fast and wet — babies are slippery. Support the body with both hands.
6. **Dry, warm, stimulate.** Immediately dry the whole baby with a towel, throw the wet towel away, and wrap in something dry including the head. Note the time of birth. Rub the back and flick the soles. Newborns lose heat terrifyingly fast and cold babies stop breathing well.
7. **Cord.** For a vigorous term newborn, wait `1 to 3 minutes` before clamping — that lets extra blood transfer from the placenta. Clamp about `6 inches` from the baby and again about `9 inches`, then cut between the clamps. Do not clamp late if the baby needs resuscitation.
8. **Placenta.** It usually comes on its own within `20 to 30 minutes`, announced by a gush of blood and the cord lengthening. Never pull the cord — you can invert the uterus and cause massive hemorrhage. Bag the placenta and bring it. Do not delay transport waiting for it.
9. **After.** Massage the fundus — the firm ball of uterus just below the belly button — with a cupped hand until it firms up. Place pads, keep her warm, encourage breastfeeding if she wants to, and reassess.

## Postpartum hemorrhage

More than `500 mL` of blood loss after delivery is hemorrhage. Almost always the uterus has failed to clamp down. Do firm fundal massage, place and count pads, keep her flat with legs elevated if she is hypotensive, high-flow oxygen, keep her warm, and transport with ALS.

> **Key:** A soft, boggy uterus after delivery is a bleeding uterus. Massage it until it feels like a grapefruit.
keyPoints: Crowning, the urge to push, or contractions 2 to 3 minutes apart lasting 60 to 90 seconds means deliver on scene.
Support the head, check for a nuchal cord, deliver the top shoulder down and the bottom shoulder up.
Dry, warm and stimulate immediately; suction only if the airway is obstructed, mouth before nose.
Clamp the cord at about 6 and 9 inches, 1 to 3 minutes after birth for a vigorous newborn.
Never pull the cord to deliver the placenta; over 500 mL of postpartum bleeding means fundal massage and rapid transport.

checks.q: You arrive to find a 24-year-old on her third pregnancy, crowning, with contractions 2 minutes apart. What is the correct action?
choices: Load and transport with lights and siren
Have her cross her legs and hold the baby in
Prepare to deliver on scene
Walk her to the ambulance to deliver en route
checks.why: Crowning means delivery is imminent, and multiparous deliveries are fast. Never delay or hold back a delivery; that injures mother and baby.

checks.q: The head has delivered and you feel the cord wrapped tightly around the neck. You cannot slip it over the head. What do you do?
choices: Clamp the cord in two places, cut between them, and deliver immediately
Pull the baby out quickly by the head
Wait for the next contraction and try again
Push the head back in and transport
checks.why: A tight nuchal cord that will not slip must be clamped and cut so the baby can be delivered. Once cut, the baby has no oxygen supply, so delivery cannot wait.

checks.q: Twenty-five minutes after delivery the placenta has not come out and the mother is stable. What should you do?
choices: Apply steady traction to the cord
Reach in and manually remove it
Transport without delay and continue fundal massage
Wait on scene until it delivers
checks.why: Pulling the cord can invert the uterus and cause catastrophic bleeding, and nothing goes in the vagina. A retained placenta is a hospital problem.

lessons.title: When delivery goes wrong
lessons.body:
Most deliveries need only clean hands and patience. These five do not. Each one has exactly one correct first move, and they are worth memorizing cold.

## Breech presentation

The buttocks or feet come first instead of the head. The body delivers, and then the head — the largest part — gets stuck in a birth canal that has not fully stretched, with the cord compressed against the pelvis.

Support the body as it delivers. Let gravity and contractions do the work. **Never pull on the baby** — traction can trap the arms over the head and make it worse. If the head does not deliver within about `3 minutes` of the body, make an airway: slide your gloved index and middle fingers into the vagina alongside the baby's face, form a **V** on either side of the nose, and push the vaginal wall away from the face so the baby can breathe. Keep your fingers there for the entire transport. Move now.

> **Key:** Breech and trapped head: fingers in a V, push the tissue off the face, do not pull, transport with your hand in place.

## Limb presentation

A single arm, leg or foot hanging out of the vagina. This baby cannot deliver vaginally in the field — ever. Do not pull it, do not push it back in. Give the mother high-flow oxygen, put her in **knee-chest** position (kneeling with chest and head down, buttocks up) to take pressure off, and transport emergently. She needs a cesarean section.

## Prolapsed cord

The cord slips down ahead of the baby and gets squeezed between the presenting part and the pelvis. Every contraction cuts the baby's oxygen supply. You have minutes.

1. Position the mother **knee-chest** or in steep **Trendelenburg** (head down, hips elevated) to let gravity pull the baby back off the cord.
2. Insert two gloved fingers into the vagina and **push the presenting part up off the cord**. Keep your hand there — through the carry, the ride, the elevator, all of it — until an obstetrician takes over at the hospital.
3. Check the cord for a pulse if you can, but do not keep handling it — that makes it spasm.
4. Cover any exposed cord with a **moist, sterile dressing** so it does not dry out.
5. High-flow oxygen to mom, transport emergently, notify the hospital early so a surgical team is waiting.

> **On the exam:** Prolapsed cord answers always contain 'keep the presenting part off the cord' and 'transport immediately.' Any choice that removes your hand is wrong.

## Shoulder dystocia

The head delivers and then retracts against the perineum — the 'turtle sign' — because the front shoulder is hung up on the pubic bone. The rest of the body will not follow.

First move is **McRoberts maneuver**: have helpers pull the mother's knees sharply back toward her chest, which rotates the pelvis and opens the outlet. Add **suprapubic pressure** — firm downward pressure just above the pubic bone by a second rescuer — to push the shoulder under. Do **not** press on the top of the uterus (fundal pressure); that jams the shoulder in harder. Do not pull hard on the head. If it does not resolve quickly, transport.

## Multiple births, meconium and prematurity

**Twins** are usually smaller, so delivery is often easier, but there are two of everything: two sets of clamps, two towels, two APGAR scores. The second baby usually arrives within `30 to 45 minutes`. Clamp the first cord before the second delivers. Expect more bleeding and more chance of prematurity.

**Meconium** — thick green-brown staining of the fluid — means the baby had a stressful moment and passed stool in the womb. If the newborn is vigorous, just dry, warm and monitor. If the newborn is depressed, do not waste time on deep suctioning: dry, warm, position, and ventilate.

**Premature infants** (before `37 weeks` or under about `5.5 pounds`) are tiny, wet and cannot hold heat at all. Dry, wrap head and body, use warm packs only over a blanket layer, keep the compartment hot, and expect to assist ventilations.
keyPoints: Breech: support, never pull; if the head is trapped over 3 minutes, make a V airway with two fingers and keep it there.
Limb presentation: no field delivery. Knee-chest, oxygen, immediate transport for cesarean section.
Prolapsed cord: knee-chest or Trendelenburg, gloved hand pushes the presenting part off the cord and stays there, moist dressing, go.
Shoulder dystocia: McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure — never fundal pressure.
Premature and meconium-stained newborns: dry, warm, position and ventilate rather than deep suction.

checks.q: You see the umbilical cord protruding from the vagina and the mother is having contractions. What is your priority action?
choices: Push the cord gently back into the vagina
Insert gloved fingers and lift the presenting part off the cord, keeping your hand in place
Clamp and cut the cord
Have the mother push with each contraction to speed delivery
checks.why: The cord is being compressed and the baby is losing oxygen. Manually lifting the presenting part restores flow; it must be maintained until surgical delivery. Never replace, clamp or cut a prolapsed cord.

checks.q: During a breech delivery the body has delivered but the head has not come out after four minutes. What do you do?
choices: Pull steadily on the baby's trunk
Push the body back in and transport
Place two gloved fingers in a V on either side of the nose to push the tissue away from the face
Have the mother stop pushing and wait
checks.why: The airway is occluded by vaginal tissue. Creating a V airway lets the baby breathe while you transport. Pulling can trap the arms and injure the spine.

checks.q: The head delivers and immediately retracts against the perineum, and the shoulders will not follow. What is the correct first maneuver?
choices: Fundal pressure on the top of the uterus
Firm downward traction on the head
McRoberts maneuver with suprapubic pressure
Knee-chest position with immediate transport
checks.why: Sharply flexing the mother's hips opens the pelvic outlet, and suprapubic pressure pushes the impacted shoulder under the pubic bone. Fundal pressure wedges it tighter.

lessons.title: Newborn care, APGAR and neonatal resuscitation
lessons.body:
Almost every newborn who looks bad simply needs to be dried, warmed and stimulated. Of the ones who need more, nearly all respond to ventilation. Newborn arrest is almost always a breathing problem, not a heart problem — which is why the newborn algorithm is nothing like the adult one.

## The first 30 seconds

Warm, dry, stimulate, position. Dry the baby vigorously with a towel, discard the wet towel, wrap in a dry one including the head, and rub the back or flick the soles of the feet. Position the airway with the head neutral or very slightly extended — a small towel roll under the shoulders keeps the big occiput from flexing the neck shut. Suction only if secretions are obstructing, mouth before nose.

Then ask three questions: is it term, is there good tone, is it breathing or crying? Three yes answers means the baby stays with the mother, skin to skin, and you just keep it warm.

> **Key:** Drying and warming is treatment, not housekeeping. A cold newborn burns oxygen and glucose making heat, gets acidotic, and stops breathing well.

## APGAR

APGAR is a score, not a treatment plan. You calculate it at `1 minute` and again at `5 minutes` after birth, but you never wait for it to start care.

| Sign | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** Appearance (color) | Blue or pale all over | Body pink, hands and feet blue | Pink all over |
| **P** Pulse | Absent | Under 100 | Over 100 |
| **G** Grimace (irritability) | No response | Grimace | Cry, cough, sneeze |
| **A** Activity (tone) | Limp | Some flexion | Active motion |
| **R** Respirations | Absent | Slow, irregular, weak cry | Strong cry |

A total of `7 to 10` is normal, `4 to 6` is moderately depressed and needs stimulation and likely ventilation, `0 to 3` needs full resuscitation.

**Worked example 1.** At one minute the baby is crying loudly, moving all four limbs, grimacing and pulling away from the bulb syringe, pulse `140`, body pink but hands and feet blue. That is Appearance 1, Pulse 2, Grimace 2, Activity 2, Respirations 2 = **9**. Blue hands and feet alone in the first minutes is normal (acrocyanosis).

**Worked example 2.** At one minute the baby is pale, limp, with a weak irregular gasp, pulse `90`, and only a faint grimace when the feet are flicked. Appearance 0, Pulse 1, Grimace 1, Activity 0, Respirations 1 = **3**. This baby needs resuscitation now.

## The resuscitation sequence

After warm-dry-stimulate-position, assess **breathing** and **heart rate**. Check the heart rate by feeling the base of the umbilical cord or listening over the chest for `6 seconds` and multiplying by `10`.

- **Breathing well and heart rate over `100`:** monitor, keep warm, reassess. Give blow-by oxygen only if central cyanosis of the trunk and lips persists.
- **Apneic, gasping, or heart rate under `100`:** start **positive-pressure ventilation** with an infant BVM at `40 to 60 breaths per minute`. Use only enough volume to make the chest barely rise. This is the single highest-yield action in newborn resuscitation.
- **Heart rate under `60` after `30 seconds` of effective ventilation:** add chest compressions. Use the **two-thumb encircling** technique — thumbs on the lower third of the sternum, fingers wrapped around the back — at a depth of one third of the chest. The ratio is `3 compressions to 1 breath`, delivering `120 events per minute`, which works out to `90 compressions and 30 breaths` each minute.
- Reassess every `30 seconds`. Stop compressions when the heart rate is over `60`; stop ventilating when the rate is over `100` and the baby is breathing on its own.

> **Trap:** The adult answer of 'start compressions' is wrong in a newborn until you have given `30 seconds` of good ventilation first. If the chest is not rising, fix the seal and the position before you add compressions.

Hypoglycemia is common in newborns, especially preterm and infants of diabetic mothers. Jitteriness, poor feeding and floppiness in a newborn should prompt a glucose check and early ALS.
keyPoints: Warm, dry, stimulate and position first — that alone fixes most depressed newborns.
APGAR is scored at 1 and 5 minutes across appearance, pulse, grimace, activity and respirations; 7 or higher is normal.
Heart rate under 100 or apnea means positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 per minute.
Heart rate under 60 after 30 seconds of good ventilation means compressions 3:1 at 120 events per minute, two-thumb technique.
Reassess every 30 seconds; newborn arrest is a ventilation problem, not a cardiac one.

checks.q: A newborn at one minute is pink on the trunk with blue hands and feet, crying strongly, actively moving, grimacing, with a pulse of 150. What is the APGAR?
checks.why: Everything scores 2 except appearance, which scores 1 for blue extremities with a pink trunk. Total is 9, which is normal; acrocyanosis is expected early.

checks.q: After 30 seconds of effective bag-valve-mask ventilation with visible chest rise, a newborn's heart rate is 52. What is the next step?
choices: Continue ventilation alone and recheck in one minute
Begin chest compressions at 3 compressions to 1 breath, 120 events per minute
Begin compressions at 30 to 2
Apply blow-by oxygen and transport
checks.why: A rate under 60 after 30 seconds of good ventilation is the trigger for compressions in a newborn, at a 3:1 ratio. The 30:2 ratio is for adults and for single-rescuer child CPR, not newborns.

checks.q: A newborn is limp and apneic immediately after delivery. What do you do first?
choices: Check a blood glucose
Deep-suction the trachea
Dry vigorously, warm, position the airway and stimulate
Start chest compressions
checks.why: The first 30 seconds are always warm, dry, stimulate and position. Most depressed newborns respond to that alone; compressions come much later in the sequence.

lessons.title: Sizing up a child: the PAT and the numbers
lessons.body:
Children compensate beautifully and then crash all at once. The skill that saves them is deciding sick or not sick in the first six seconds, from the doorway, before you ever touch them — because touching a sick child makes them cry, and a crying child hides everything.

## The pediatric assessment triangle

The PAT has three arms, all done by looking and listening from a distance.

**Appearance** — is the brain getting what it needs? Use TICLS: **T**one (are they moving, or floppy), **I**nteractiveness (do they reach, play, track you), **C**onsolability (does the caregiver settle them), **L**ook or gaze (do the eyes fix on you, or stare through you), **S**peech or cry (strong, or weak and whimpering). An abnormal appearance means poor brain perfusion, low oxygen, low glucose, a toxin, or a head injury.

**Work of breathing** — is air moving? Listen for noises without a stethoscope: snoring, stridor, grunting, wheezing. Look for position (tripod, sniffing), nasal flaring, head bobbing, and retractions — skin sucking in between ribs, above the collarbones, below the sternum. Abnormal work of breathing means a respiratory problem.

**Circulation to skin** — is blood reaching the surface? Look for pallor, mottling (blotchy marbled skin) and cyanosis. Abnormal circulation to skin means shock or blood loss.

Now combine them:

| Appearance | Breathing | Skin | Impression |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | Abnormal | Normal | Respiratory distress |
| Abnormal | Abnormal | Normal | Respiratory failure |
| Normal | Normal | Abnormal | Compensated shock |
| Abnormal | Normal | Abnormal | Decompensated shock |
| Abnormal | Normal | Normal | Brain problem: seizure, glucose, toxin, head injury |
| Abnormal | Abnormal | Abnormal | Cardiopulmonary failure — act now |

> **Key:** All three arms abnormal is a child who is minutes from arrest. Open the airway, ventilate, and move.

## Normal vitals by age

The single most tested table in pediatrics. Notice two things: rates fall and pressure rises as they grow.

| Age | Respirations | Heart rate | Systolic BP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Newborn | 30-60 | 100-180 | 60-90 |
| Infant (1-12 mo) | 25-50 | 100-160 | 70-95 |
| Toddler (1-3 yr) | 20-30 | 90-150 | 80-100 |
| Preschool (4-5 yr) | 20-28 | 80-140 | 80-100 |
| School age (6-12 yr) | 18-25 | 70-120 | 80-110 |
| Adolescent (13-18 yr) | 12-20 | 60-100 | 90-110 |

A rough floor for the minimum acceptable systolic pressure in a child aged `1 to 10` is `70 plus twice the age in years`. For a 4-year-old that is `78 mmHg` — anything below it is decompensated shock.

> **Trap:** Bradycardia in a child is a dying sign, not a calm one. A heart rate of `55` in a 2-year-old means hypoxia until proven otherwise — ventilate, do not congratulate.

## Airway and ventilation differences

Children have a large head, a big tongue, a small floppy airway, and nostrils they depend on for breathing when very young. That drives the technique:

- Keep the head **neutral** in infants and only slightly extended in small children. Over-extending kinks the soft trachea shut. Pad under the shoulders, not the head.
- Use a mask that covers nose and mouth without touching the eyes or hanging past the chin.
- Ventilate at `1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds` (about `20 to 30` per minute) for infants and children with a pulse. Squeeze only until the chest starts to rise — over-inflation causes gastric distension, which pushes up on the diaphragm and makes everything worse.
- A nasal cannula at `2 to 4 L/min` or blow-by oxygen is often better tolerated than a mask jammed on a screaming face, and a calm child moves more air than a fighting one.
keyPoints: The PAT is appearance, work of breathing and circulation to skin — done from the doorway before you touch the child.
Abnormal appearance means brain perfusion, oxygen, glucose or toxin; abnormal breathing means respiratory; abnormal skin means shock.
Rates fall and blood pressure rises with age; minimum systolic for ages 1 to 10 is 70 plus twice the age.
Bradycardia in a child means hypoxia until proven otherwise — ventilate immediately.
Ventilate a child at 1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds, just enough for chest rise, head neutral in infants.

checks.q: A 3-year-old has a normal appearance and normal skin color but is grunting with intercostal retractions. What is your impression?
choices: Compensated shock
Respiratory distress
Respiratory failure
Cardiopulmonary failure
checks.why: Only work of breathing is abnormal, so the child is compensating. If appearance became abnormal too, that would be respiratory failure and would demand immediate ventilation.

checks.q: A 2-year-old struck by a car has a heart rate of 50 and shallow breathing. What does the heart rate most likely indicate?
choices: A normal response to a head injury
Well-controlled pain
Severe hypoxia, requiring immediate ventilation
A vagal response to fear
checks.why: Children become bradycardic from hypoxia, and it is a pre-arrest sign. The treatment is oxygenation and ventilation, not observation.

checks.q: What is the minimum acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 6-year-old?
choices: 70 mmHg
76 mmHg
82 mmHg
90 mmHg
checks.why: The formula for ages 1 to 10 is 70 plus twice the age in years: 70 plus 12 equals 82 mmHg. Below that is decompensated shock.

lessons.title: Pediatric emergencies you will actually see
lessons.body:
## Noisy airways: croup versus epiglottitis

Both are upper-airway swelling in a child who cannot breathe well. Telling them apart changes what you do with your hands.

| | Croup | Epiglottitis |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Virus, swelling below the cords | Bacterial infection of the epiglottis |
| Age | `6 months to 3 years` | Any age, often `3 to 7 years` |
| Onset | Over a day or two, worse at night | Hours, rapidly worsening |
| Cough | Harsh, barking, seal-like | Usually none |
| Classic look | Stridor when upset, low fever | Drooling, tripod position, muffled 'hot potato' voice, high fever, looks toxic |

Croup gets humidified or blow-by oxygen, a calm parent's lap, cool night air, and transport. Epiglottitis gets nothing in the mouth: **no tongue depressor, no oral airway, no throat inspection, no IV attempts in the field**. Any of those can cause total airway spasm. Let the child sit however they want, give blow-by oxygen, keep them calm, and transport gently with ALS.

> **Key:** Drooling plus tripod plus no cough equals hands off the throat and a quiet, fast ride.

## Lower airway: bronchiolitis and asthma

**Bronchiolitis** (usually RSV) clogs the smallest airways of infants under `2`: wheezing, crackles, poor feeding, and apnea in the youngest. Suction the nose — infants breathe through it — give oxygen, transport.

**Asthma** is bronchospasm plus mucus in a child usually over `2` with a history. Wheezing that disappears in a child who is still working hard is not improvement — it means no air is moving. Assist with the patient's own metered-dose inhaler or nebulizer per protocol, give oxygen, and let them sit up.

## Fever, seizures and infection

A **febrile seizure** happens in about `1 in 25` children between `6 months and 6 years`, usually with a fast rise in temperature. Most are brief and generalized. Protect the child, keep the airway open, do not restrain, remove heavy clothing, and transport — every first-time seizure needs evaluation.

**Fever in an infant under 3 months is an emergency.** Their immune systems cannot wall off infection, and a rectal temperature at or above `100.4 F (38 C)` needs a full hospital work-up regardless of how well they look.

**Meningitis** signs: fever plus severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, a bulging fontanelle in an infant, a high-pitched cry, and a purple non-blanching rash (petechiae) that does not fade under pressure. That rash with a fever is a load-and-go with a mask on the patient and on you.

## Dehydration and shock

Children lose fluid fast from vomiting and diarrhea and hold pressure until the very end.

- **Mild:** slightly dry lips, normal vitals, normal urine.
- **Moderate:** dry mouth, sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle in infants, fewer wet diapers, capillary refill `2 to 3 seconds`, tachycardia.
- **Severe:** lethargy, no tears, skin tenting, capillary refill over `3 seconds`, cool mottled skin, very few or no wet diapers.

> **Trap:** A child's blood pressure stays normal through compensated shock and drops only after `30 to 45%` volume loss. When the pressure falls, arrest is close. Grade shock by heart rate, capillary refill, skin and mental status.

## SIDS, BRUE, poisoning and drowning

**SIDS** is the sudden death of an apparently healthy infant under `1 year`. Resuscitate unless there are obvious signs of irreversible death, disturb the scene as little as possible, and use plain, blameless language with the family.

**BRUE** is an infant who briefly stopped breathing, changed color or went limp and now looks normal. Normal now does not mean fine — transport every one.

**Poisoning** is a toddler problem: ask what, how much and when, and bring the container. **Drowning** children are hypoxic first, so ventilation leads, and cold water justifies prolonged resuscitation.

## Abuse and neglect

The red flags are pattern-based, not dramatic:

- The injury does not match the story, or the story keeps changing.
- The injury does not match the child's developmental stage — infants who cannot roll do not fall off beds.
- Patterned bruises (loop, hand, belt), bruises on the torso, ears or neck, cigarette burns, stocking or glove burns with clean lines.
- Delayed care for a serious injury.
- A child who is watchful, withdrawn, or indifferent to the caregiver.

You do not investigate, accuse, or confront. You document exactly what you saw and exactly what was said, in quotes. In **New Jersey**, every person is a mandated reporter and reports go to the Division of Child Protection and Permanency (DCP&P) at `1-877-NJ-ABUSE (1-877-652-2873)`. Notify the receiving hospital as well.

> **On shift:** Write the facts, not your conclusion. 'Three-inch curved bruise on left flank; mother states child fell from couch' is useful. 'Suspected abuse' alone is not.
keyPoints: Croup barks and has stridor; epiglottitis drools and tripods — never put anything in the mouth of a suspected epiglottitis.
Fever in an infant under 3 months, or a non-blanching purple rash with fever, is a true emergency.
Grade pediatric dehydration and shock by heart rate, capillary refill, skin and mental status — blood pressure falls last.
Every first febrile seizure and every BRUE gets transported even if the child looks fine now.
Abuse red flags: injury versus story mismatch, developmentally impossible injuries, patterned bruises, delayed care; report to DCP&P at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE.

checks.q: A 4-year-old with a high fever is sitting forward, drooling, with a muffled voice and no cough. What must you avoid?
choices: Blow-by oxygen
Letting the child sit in a parent's lap
Examining the throat with a tongue depressor
Calling for ALS
checks.why: This is epiglottitis. Manipulating the throat can trigger complete airway obstruction. Keep the child calm and upright, give blow-by oxygen, and transport gently.

checks.q: A 5-month-old with two days of vomiting is lethargic, has sunken eyes, no tears, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and a BP of 82/54. How do you classify this?
choices: Mild dehydration, since the BP is normal
Severe dehydration with compensated shock
Normal findings for an infant
Respiratory failure
checks.why: Lethargy, no tears and capillary refill over 3 seconds are severe dehydration. A normal blood pressure in a child means compensation, not stability — it drops only after 30 to 45% volume loss.

checks.q: You suspect child abuse. What is the correct action in New Jersey?
choices: Confront the caregiver on scene to get the truth
Document objective findings and statements, report to DCP&P at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE, and notify the receiving hospital
Wait for a physician to confirm abuse before reporting
Only report if the injury is life-threatening
checks.why: New Jersey makes every person a mandated reporter, and suspicion is enough — confirmation is not required. Confronting the caregiver endangers the crew and the child.

lessons.title: Geriatrics and patients with special challenges
lessons.body:
Older patients present sideways. The classic textbook presentation belongs to a 40-year-old; by `75`, disease shows up as weakness, confusion or a fall, and the crushing chest pain never comes.

## Why the picture blurs

Nerves conduct pain less sharply, so a heart attack can be painless — a **silent MI** that shows up as sudden shortness of breath, fatigue, nausea or new confusion. Diabetics and women are especially likely to present this way.

The fever response weakens, so an older patient with a serious infection (sepsis) can be `98.6 F` or even cool, with confusion and a low blood pressure as the only clues. The immune system, thermoregulation and thirst drive all decline together.

Cardiac output falls, arteries stiffen, and lung reserve drops, so compensation is thin. Kidneys clear drugs more slowly, so medications accumulate.

> **Key:** In an older patient, 'weak and confused' is a chief complaint that means sepsis, MI, stroke, bleed, low sugar or a medication problem until you have ruled them out.

## Polypharmacy

Many older patients take `5 to 15` medications prescribed by several doctors who never talk to each other. Drugs interact, dosing errors happen, and a new symptom is often just a new prescription.

Take the whole bag of pill bottles, or a photo of the list. It is history, allergy list and problem list in one. Key items that change your thinking: **beta blockers** (blunt the tachycardia of shock, so a heart rate of `70` in a bleeding patient means nothing reassuring), **anticoagulants** such as warfarin, apixaban or clopidogrel (a head strike becomes a potential brain bleed), **insulin and oral diabetes drugs**, **diuretics** (dehydration, low potassium), and **digoxin** (nausea, visual halos, arrhythmias when levels drift up).

## Falls, dementia and delirium

A fall is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Ask why: did the room spin, did they black out, did the leg give out, did a new blood-pressure pill start last week? Mechanical trips and syncope look identical on arrival and mean completely different things.

| | Dementia | Delirium |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Months to years | Hours to days |
| Course | Steady, slowly worsening | Fluctuates through the day |
| Attention | Relatively preserved early | Poor, cannot follow a thread |
| Cause | Chronic brain disease | Infection, hypoxia, drugs, glucose, pain |

> **Trap:** 'The patient has dementia' is not a reason to accept confusion. Ask the family the one question that matters: is this how she normally is? A sudden change is delirium, and delirium is a medical emergency.

Bones thin (osteoporosis) so a low fall breaks hips, and skin thins so tape and straps tear it. Pad everything, use gentle traction, and never force a joint that is contracted. Hearing and vision loss are not confusion: face them, speak low and slow, and bring their glasses and hearing aids.

**Elder abuse** looks like bruising in different stages of healing, pressure ulcers, malnutrition, poor hygiene, missing medications, or a caregiver who answers every question for the patient. Report it like child abuse; in New Jersey, Adult Protective Services handles it.

Finally, know the paperwork. A **DNR** or a **POLST** form states what the patient wants. A valid DNR means no resuscitation; it never means no care — comfort, oxygen, positioning and transport all continue. If the form is not present, is not valid, or family objects, begin resuscitation and sort it out with medical direction.

## Patients with special challenges

- **Tracheostomy:** a surgical airway at the neck. Suction the tube (`5 to 10 seconds`, on the way out) if it is plugged, and ventilate through the trach with a BVM if the patient is in distress. Families often know the routine better than you do.
- **Home ventilators:** if the machine alarms and the patient is in distress, disconnect the vent and bag them through the trach. Bring the machine and the settings.
- **VP shunts:** drain fluid from the brain to the abdomen. A blocked shunt causes headache, vomiting, lethargy and irritability — high-priority transport.
- **Feeding tubes** (G-tube, PEG, NG): nothing goes down them; watch for aspiration and keep the head elevated.
- **Central lines and ports:** long-term IV access. Do not use them, do not draw from them, keep the site clean, and tell the hospital it is there.
- **Bariatric patients:** call for extra hands and the right stretcher early, never improvise a lift, and expect breathing difficulty when flat.
- **Developmental disability:** address the patient, not the caregiver. Simple sentences, one instruction at a time. Ask the caregiver what is normal for this person.
- **Hearing or vision loss:** get in their line of sight, ask if they read lips, write things down, and describe each step before you do it.
keyPoints: Older patients present atypically: silent MI, sepsis without fever, and weakness or confusion as the only symptom.
Bring the medication bag; beta blockers hide tachycardia and anticoagulants turn a head strike into a bleed.
A fall is a symptom — find out why it happened.
Sudden confusion is delirium and a medical emergency; dementia is slow and chronic.
A valid DNR or POLST limits resuscitation, never comfort care, oxygen, positioning or transport.

checks.q: An 82-year-old is brought in for 'just not acting right' since this morning. She is afebrile, HR 96, BP 104/62, and her daughter says she was sharp yesterday. What should you suspect?
choices: Normal aging
Progression of dementia
An acute problem such as sepsis, MI or a medication effect
Anxiety
checks.why: A sudden change from baseline is delirium, not dementia, and in an older patient it commonly means infection, cardiac ischemia, hypoxia, low glucose or a drug effect. Absent fever does not rule out sepsis.

checks.q: A 78-year-old on metoprolol has a GI bleed. His heart rate is 74 and BP is 96/58. How should you interpret the heart rate?
choices: Reassuring evidence that he is not in shock
Unreliable, because the beta blocker prevents the compensatory tachycardia
Evidence of a vagal response
Proof that the reported bleeding is minor
checks.why: Beta blockers block the heart-rate response to blood loss. Judge perfusion by skin, mental status, capillary refill and pressure trend instead, and treat for shock.

checks.q: A patient with a home ventilator is in distress and the machine is alarming. What should you do?
choices: Adjust the ventilator settings until the alarm stops
Disconnect the ventilator and ventilate through the tracheostomy with a bag-valve mask
Remove the tracheostomy tube and ventilate through the mouth
Wait for the home-care company to respond
checks.why: When the machine and the patient disagree, take the machine out of the equation and bag the patient through the existing airway. EMTs do not adjust ventilator settings.

cards.front: By how much does blood volume increase in pregnancy, and why does it matter?
cards.back: About 50 percent, roughly 1 to 1.5 liters extra. She can lose about 1,500 mL before the blood pressure falls, so shock appears late and normal vitals are falsely reassuring.

cards.front: What is supine hypotensive syndrome and how do you fix it?
cards.back: After about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when she lies flat, dropping venous return and blood pressure. Fix: tilt 15 to 30 degrees left, or manually displace the uterus.

cards.front: Why is aspiration risk higher in a pregnant patient?
cards.back: Hormones relax the lower esophageal sphincter, gastric emptying slows, and the uterus raises abdominal pressure. Keep suction on and ventilate gently to avoid inflating the stomach.

cards.front: What happens to heart rate, blood pressure and respiratory rate in normal pregnancy?
cards.back: Heart rate rises 10 to 15 beats per minute, blood pressure drops 5 to 15 mmHg in the second trimester, and breathing is faster and shallower. A respiratory rate over 24 is abnormal.

cards.front: What is the guiding principle for trauma in pregnancy?
cards.back: Treat the mother. High-flow oxygen, bleeding control, warmth, left tilt, spinal precautions if indicated, and transport to a trauma center. Every pregnant trauma patient past 20 weeks goes in.

cards.front: How do you tilt a pregnant patient who is secured to a long backboard?
cards.back: Tilt the entire board 15 to 30 degrees to the left by padding under the right side, keeping her spine aligned. Alternatively displace the uterus up and left by hand.

cards.front: What is the classic presentation of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy?
cards.back: Missed period, one-sided lower abdominal pain, light or absent vaginal bleeding, referred shoulder pain from blood on the diaphragm, and signs of shock. Leading cause of first-trimester death.

cards.front: How do you tell placenta previa from abruptio placentae?
cards.back: Previa: painless, bright red bleeding, soft uterus. Abruption: painful, dark red bleeding, rigid tender uterus, often after trauma, and the bleeding may be entirely concealed.

cards.front: What must never be done for vaginal bleeding in pregnancy?
cards.back: Never place anything in the vagina — no packing, no internal exam. Apply external pads, count them to estimate loss, give oxygen, keep her warm, tilt left, transport.

cards.front: What defines preeclampsia?
cards.back: After 20 weeks: blood pressure 140/90 or higher plus protein in the urine, with headache, vision changes, facial and hand swelling, upper-right abdominal pain and brisk reflexes.

cards.front: How do you manage an eclamptic seizure?
cards.back: Protect from injury without restraining, left lateral position, suction, high-flow oxygen after the seizure, keep the compartment dim and quiet, and transport rapidly to an obstetric hospital.

cards.front: How long after delivery can eclampsia still occur?
cards.back: Up to 6 weeks postpartum. A recently delivered patient with a seizure, headache or vision changes is an eclampsia call until proven otherwise.

cards.front: Which three findings mean delivery is imminent?
cards.back: Crowning, an overwhelming urge to push or to move the bowels, and contractions 2 to 3 minutes apart lasting 60 to 90 seconds. Crowning alone decides it: deliver on scene.

cards.front: What belongs in an OB kit?
cards.back: Sterile gloves, drapes and towels, two cord clamps, scissors or scalpel, bulb syringe, gauze, a bag for the placenta, an infant blanket or swaddler, and sanitary pads.

cards.front: How do you control the head during delivery?
cards.back: Place a flat gloved hand on the crowning head with gentle pressure so it emerges slowly. Never pull, and never press on the fontanelle. Slow delivery prevents tearing and injury.

cards.front: What do you do about a nuchal cord?
cards.back: Check as soon as the head delivers. If loose, slip it over the head. If tight and unslippable, clamp it twice, cut between the clamps, and deliver the baby immediately.

cards.front: When and how do you suction a newborn at delivery?
cards.back: Only if secretions obstruct the airway or the baby needs ventilation. Squeeze the bulb first, then suction mouth before nose. Routine suctioning of vigorous newborns is no longer recommended.

cards.front: How are the shoulders delivered?
cards.back: Support the head and guide it gently downward to free the anterior (top) shoulder, then gently upward for the posterior (bottom) shoulder. The body then slides out fast — hold on.

cards.front: Where and when do you clamp and cut the cord?
cards.back: For a vigorous term newborn, wait 1 to 3 minutes. Clamp about 6 inches from the baby and again at about 9 inches, then cut between the clamps.

cards.front: What are the rules for delivering the placenta?
cards.back: It usually comes within 20 to 30 minutes. Never pull the cord — that can invert the uterus. Bag it and bring it, and never delay transport waiting for it.

cards.front: How much postpartum bleeding counts as hemorrhage, and what do you do?
cards.back: More than 500 mL. Massage the fundus until firm, place and count pads, keep her warm and flat with legs elevated if hypotensive, high-flow oxygen, rapid transport with ALS.

cards.front: What does a soft boggy uterus after delivery mean?
cards.back: The uterus has not clamped down on its torn vessels, so it is bleeding. Massage the fundus with a cupped hand until it feels firm like a grapefruit.

cards.front: How do you manage a breech delivery?
cards.back: Support the body as it delivers, never pull. If the head is not out within about 3 minutes, place two gloved fingers in a V beside the nose to push tissue off the face.

cards.front: What do you do for a limb presentation?
cards.back: Nothing vaginal. Do not pull the limb or push it back. Oxygen, knee-chest position, and immediate transport — this baby needs a cesarean section.

cards.front: List the steps for a prolapsed umbilical cord.
cards.back: Knee-chest or Trendelenburg, insert two gloved fingers to lift the presenting part off the cord and keep the hand there, moist sterile dressing over exposed cord, oxygen, emergent transport.

cards.front: What is the turtle sign and what does it mean?
cards.back: The head delivers then retracts against the perineum. It signals shoulder dystocia — the anterior shoulder is caught on the pubic bone.

cards.front: How do you manage shoulder dystocia?
cards.back: McRoberts maneuver: sharply flex the mother's knees back to her chest. Add suprapubic pressure from a second rescuer. Never use fundal pressure and never pull hard on the head.

cards.front: What should you expect with twin deliveries?
cards.back: Two sets of clamps, towels and APGAR scores. Clamp the first cord before the second delivers. The second baby usually arrives in 30 to 45 minutes. Expect prematurity and more bleeding.

cards.front: What does meconium-stained fluid mean and how do you respond?
cards.back: The baby passed stool in the womb from stress. Vigorous newborn: dry, warm, monitor. Depressed newborn: dry, warm, position and ventilate — do not delay for deep suctioning.

cards.front: What is the biggest immediate threat to a premature newborn?
cards.back: Heat loss. Born before 37 weeks or under about 5.5 pounds, they cannot maintain temperature. Dry, wrap head and body, heat the compartment, and expect to assist ventilations.

cards.front: What are the first four actions for every newborn?
cards.back: Warm, dry, stimulate, position. Dry vigorously, discard the wet towel, wrap including the head, rub the back or flick the soles, and keep the head neutral with a shoulder roll.

cards.front: What do the five letters of APGAR stand for?
cards.back: Appearance (color), Pulse, Grimace (irritability), Activity (tone), Respirations. Each scores 0, 1 or 2, at 1 minute and again at 5 minutes after birth.

cards.front: How do you interpret an APGAR total?
cards.back: 7 to 10 is normal, 4 to 6 is moderately depressed and needs stimulation and probably ventilation, 0 to 3 needs full resuscitation. Never delay care to calculate it.

cards.front: A newborn is pink centrally with blue hands and feet, crying, moving, grimacing, pulse 150. APGAR?
cards.back: 9. Everything scores 2 except appearance, which scores 1. Blue hands and feet alone (acrocyanosis) is normal in the first minutes of life.

cards.front: At what newborn heart rate do you start positive-pressure ventilation, and at what rate?
cards.back: Heart rate under 100, or apnea or gasping. Ventilate at 40 to 60 breaths per minute with just enough volume for the chest to barely rise.

cards.front: When do you start chest compressions on a newborn?
cards.back: Heart rate under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation with visible chest rise. Not before — fix the seal and airway position first.

cards.front: What is the newborn compression ratio, rate and technique?
cards.back: 3 compressions to 1 breath, 120 events per minute (90 compressions and 30 breaths each minute), two-thumb encircling technique on the lower third of the sternum, one third chest depth.

cards.front: How do you check a newborn's heart rate quickly?
cards.back: Feel the base of the umbilical cord or listen over the chest for 6 seconds and multiply by 10. Reassess every 30 seconds during resuscitation.

cards.front: Why is newborn arrest treated as a breathing problem?
cards.back: Newborn hearts are healthy; they fail from hypoxia. That is why ventilation comes before compressions and why the ratio is 3:1 rather than 30:2.

cards.front: What are the three arms of the pediatric assessment triangle?
cards.back: Appearance (brain perfusion), work of breathing (respiratory status), and circulation to skin (perfusion). All three are assessed by looking and listening from the doorway.

cards.front: What does TICLS stand for in assessing a child's appearance?
cards.back: Tone, Interactiveness, Consolability, Look or gaze, and Speech or cry. Abnormal appearance means poor brain perfusion, hypoxia, low glucose, a toxin or head injury.

cards.front: Normal appearance, abnormal work of breathing, normal skin — what is the impression?
cards.back: Respiratory distress. If appearance also becomes abnormal, it has progressed to respiratory failure and demands immediate assisted ventilation.

cards.front: What are normal heart rate and respiratory rate for an infant under 1 year?
cards.back: Heart rate 100 to 160, respirations 25 to 50, systolic blood pressure roughly 70 to 95 mmHg.

cards.front: What is the minimum acceptable systolic blood pressure formula for children 1 to 10 years?
cards.back: 70 plus twice the age in years. A 4-year-old needs at least 78 mmHg; below that is decompensated shock.

cards.front: What does bradycardia mean in a child?
cards.back: Hypoxia until proven otherwise, and a pre-arrest sign. The treatment is oxygenation and assisted ventilation, not observation.

cards.front: How do pediatric airway anatomy differences change your technique?
cards.back: Large head, big tongue, soft narrow trachea: keep the head neutral in infants, pad under the shoulders not the head, and avoid hyperextension, which kinks the airway shut.

cards.front: What is the BVM ventilation rate for an infant or child with a pulse?
cards.back: One breath every 2 to 3 seconds, about 20 to 30 per minute. Squeeze only until the chest starts to rise; over-inflation distends the stomach and worsens ventilation.

cards.front: How do croup and epiglottitis differ?
cards.back: Croup: viral, barking cough, stridor when upset, gradual onset, ages 6 months to 3 years. Epiglottitis: bacterial, drooling, tripod, muffled voice, high fever, no cough, rapid onset.

cards.front: What must you never do with suspected epiglottitis?
cards.back: Nothing in the mouth: no tongue depressor, no oral airway, no throat inspection, no agitating procedures. Keep the child calm and upright, blow-by oxygen, gentle rapid transport.

cards.front: Why is a nasal suction so important in an infant with bronchiolitis?
cards.back: Infants breathe mainly through the nose, so a plugged nose is an obstructed airway. Suction the nares, give oxygen, and transport; RSV bronchiolitis can cause apnea in the youngest.

cards.front: Why is fever in an infant under 3 months an emergency?
cards.back: Their immune systems cannot contain infection. A rectal temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher needs a full hospital work-up regardless of how well the infant appears.

cards.front: What are the signs of severe dehydration in a child?
cards.back: Lethargy, no tears, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes or fontanelle, skin tenting, capillary refill over 3 seconds, cool mottled skin, and very few or no wet diapers.

cards.front: Why is blood pressure a poor way to judge shock in a child?
cards.back: Children compensate with vasoconstriction and tachycardia and hold a normal pressure until 30 to 45 percent volume loss. When pressure falls, arrest is near.

cards.front: What is a BRUE and what do you do about it?
cards.back: A brief resolved unexplained event: an infant who briefly stopped breathing, changed color or went limp and is now normal. Transport every one; normal now does not mean fine.

cards.front: What rash with fever demands immediate transport in a child?
cards.back: A purple, non-blanching petechial rash that does not fade under pressure — a sign of meningococcal disease. Mask the patient and yourself and move fast.

cards.front: List five red flags for child abuse.
cards.back: Injury does not match the story, injury is developmentally impossible, patterned bruises (loop, hand, belt), burns with clean lines, delayed care, and a withdrawn or watchful child.

cards.front: Who do you call to report suspected child abuse in New Jersey?
cards.back: The Division of Child Protection and Permanency (DCP&P) at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE (1-877-652-2873). Every person in New Jersey is a mandated reporter; suspicion is enough.

cards.front: Why can a heart attack be painless in an older patient?
cards.back: Pain perception dulls with age and with diabetes. A silent MI shows up as sudden shortness of breath, fatigue, nausea, weakness or new confusion instead of chest pain.

cards.front: Why can an older patient with sepsis have a normal temperature?
cards.back: The fever response weakens with age, so serious infection may present with confusion, weakness and hypotension while the temperature is normal or even low.

cards.front: How do you distinguish delirium from dementia?
cards.back: Delirium starts in hours to days, fluctuates, and destroys attention; dementia develops over months to years and is steady. Sudden change from baseline is delirium — a medical emergency.

cards.front: Which two medication classes most change your assessment of an older patient?
cards.back: Beta blockers, which prevent the tachycardia of shock, and anticoagulants or antiplatelets, which turn a minor head strike into a potential brain bleed.

cards.front: Why is a fall in an older patient never just a fall?
cards.back: It is a symptom. Ask why: syncope, dizziness, a new medication, weakness, an arrhythmia, low sugar, infection or poor vision. The cause matters more than the bruise.

cards.front: What does a valid DNR or POLST actually change?
cards.back: It limits resuscitation only. Comfort measures, oxygen, positioning, pain relief and transport all continue. If the form is absent, invalid or disputed, begin resuscitation and contact medical direction.

cards.front: A home ventilator is alarming and the patient is in distress. What do you do?
cards.back: Disconnect the ventilator and ventilate through the tracheostomy with a bag-valve mask. EMTs do not adjust ventilator settings. Bring the machine and the settings to the hospital.

cards.front: What are the signs of a blocked VP shunt?
cards.back: Headache, vomiting, lethargy, irritability and altered mental status as pressure builds in the brain. Treat it as a high-priority transport.

cards.front: What are the rules about a patient's central line or implanted port?
cards.back: Do not use it, do not draw from it, do not flush it. Keep the site clean and covered, and tell the receiving hospital it exists.

quiz.q: A 32-week pregnant woman is restrained driver in a moderate-speed collision. She is alert, BP 118/72, HR 106, and complains of mild abdominal soreness. What is your greatest concern?
choices: She is stable and can refuse transport after a normal exam
Significant internal or placental bleeding may be present despite normal vital signs
Her heart rate of 106 indicates anxiety and nothing more
Fetal injury is the main issue and should guide treatment
quiz.why: Increased blood volume and uterine shunting keep the blood pressure normal until roughly a third of volume is lost, and abruption can be entirely concealed. The mildly elevated heart rate is the early sign. Treating the fetus directly is never an EMT option; treating the mother is.

quiz.q: After what gestational age should a pregnant patient be tilted onto her left side when supine?
choices: About 20 weeks
About 8 weeks
Only at full term
Only if she reports dizziness
quiz.why: Around 20 weeks the fundus reaches the umbilicus and the uterus is heavy enough to compress the inferior vena cava. Waiting for symptoms means she has already dropped her cardiac output; tilt preemptively.

quiz.q: A 36-week pregnant patient placed supine becomes pale and diaphoretic with a BP of 84/48. What is the correct immediate action?
choices: Apply high-flow oxygen and continue transport supine
Sit her fully upright in the captain's chair
Tilt her 15 to 30 degrees onto her left side
Begin assisted ventilation with a bag-valve mask
quiz.why: This is mechanical obstruction of the vena cava, so the treatment is mechanical: left tilt restores venous return in seconds. Oxygen alone does not fix an emptying heart, and she is breathing adequately so BVM is unnecessary.

quiz.q: A 33-week pregnant woman has sudden, bright red, painless vaginal bleeding. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Abruptio placentae
Preterm labor
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Placenta previa
quiz.why: Painless, bright red bleeding with a soft uterus is the previa pattern, where the placenta covers the cervix. Abruption is painful with a rigid uterus, and ectopic pregnancy ruptures in the first trimester, not at 33 weeks.

quiz.q: A 30-week pregnant patient was punched in the abdomen. She has constant severe abdominal pain, a rigid tender uterus, and only a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. Why is this dangerous?
choices: The small amount of bleeding shows the injury is minor
Most of the blood loss may be concealed behind the placenta
Uterine rigidity confirms she is in normal labor
Dark blood means it is old and no longer active
quiz.why: In abruptio placentae the placenta shears off the uterine wall and blood collects behind it, so external bleeding badly underestimates the loss. Rigidity and constant pain distinguish abruption from labor, which comes in waves.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old woman has severe left lower abdominal pain, a missed period, light spotting, and pain in her left shoulder. She is pale with a HR of 122. What do you suspect?
choices: Ovarian cyst
Urinary tract infection
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Placenta previa
quiz.why: One-sided pain with a missed period plus referred shoulder pain from blood irritating the diaphragm is classic ruptured ectopic, and the tachycardia and pallor mean she is bleeding into the abdomen. Cysts and infections do not cause referred shoulder pain with shock.

quiz.q: Which set of findings best fits preeclampsia?
choices: 26 weeks, BP 92/58, dizziness on standing, no edema
34 weeks, BP 132/84, painless bright red bleeding
14 weeks, BP 146/92, nausea and vomiting all morning
28 weeks, BP 168/104, severe headache, blurred vision, swollen hands and face
quiz.why: Preeclampsia requires a blood pressure of 140/90 or higher after 20 weeks with symptoms such as headache, vision changes and edema. A high pressure at 14 weeks is chronic hypertension, not preeclampsia, and painless bleeding is previa.

quiz.q: You are transporting a 34-week pregnant patient who just had a generalized seizure. Which combination of actions is correct?
choices: Supine with restraints, bright lights, siren on for speed
Left lateral, suction ready, oxygen, lights dimmed and minimal noise
Fully upright with a cold pack to the forehead and oral glucose
Supine with a nasal cannula and a blood pressure check every 30 seconds
quiz.why: Eclampsia care is airway protection in the left lateral position with suction and oxygen, and minimizing stimulation because light, noise and motion can trigger another seizure. Restraints cause injury, and glucose is for hypoglycemia, not eclampsia.

quiz.q: Which finding most definitively means you should prepare to deliver on scene?
choices: Crowning at the vaginal opening
Rupture of membranes one hour ago
Contractions every 7 minutes
This is her first pregnancy and she feels pressure
quiz.why: Crowning means the head is at the outlet and delivery cannot be delayed. Contractions 7 minutes apart and ruptured membranes alone still allow transport, and first pregnancies typically progress slowly.

quiz.q: A woman on her fourth pregnancy is crowning with contractions 2 minutes apart, 10 minutes from the hospital. What should you do?
choices: Prepare to deliver where you are
Transport emergently and deliver in the hospital driveway
Have her hold her legs together until arrival
Transport her seated upright to slow the delivery
quiz.why: Crowning plus a multiparous patient means the baby is coming in minutes. Delaying or physically holding back a delivery risks fetal hypoxia and maternal injury, and delivering in a moving ambulance is more dangerous than delivering on a controlled scene.

quiz.q: The head has delivered and you find the cord looped once around the neck but loose. What is the correct action?
choices: Clamp and cut it immediately
Apply traction on the shoulders to free it
Leave it alone and deliver the shoulders through it
Gently slip it over the baby's head
quiz.why: A loose nuchal cord is slipped over the head so the baby delivers with the placental circulation intact. Clamping and cutting is reserved for a cord too tight to slip, because once cut the baby has no oxygen source.

quiz.q: Where should the two cord clamps be placed on a newborn?
choices: At 2 and 4 inches from the baby
At 6 and 9 inches from the baby
At 12 and 15 inches from the baby
Directly against the abdominal wall and again at 3 inches
quiz.why: The standard placement is roughly 6 inches from the newborn and a second clamp about 9 inches out, cutting between them. Clamping against the abdomen risks injury, and clamping too far out leaves excess cord.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes after delivery the placenta has not delivered. The mother is alert with stable vitals. What is the correct action?
choices: Apply gentle continuous traction to the umbilical cord
Manually remove the placenta
Continue transport and perform fundal massage
Stay on scene until the placenta delivers
quiz.why: Traction on the cord can invert the uterus and cause catastrophic hemorrhage, and nothing is inserted into the vagina in the field. A retained placenta is managed at the hospital, so transport and keep the fundus firm.

quiz.q: After delivery the mother has soaked three large pads in ten minutes and her uterus feels soft. What is your first intervention?
choices: Massage the fundus until it becomes firm
Pack the vagina with sterile gauze
Place her in Trendelenburg and wait
Apply a tourniquet high on each thigh
quiz.why: A boggy uterus means the muscle has not clamped the torn vessels shut, and fundal massage is the direct fix. Vaginal packing is never done by EMS, and tourniquets do nothing for uterine bleeding.

quiz.q: A breech delivery has progressed to the shoulders, but the head remains undelivered after four minutes. What should you do?
choices: Apply firm downward traction on the trunk
Have the mother stop pushing and transport without intervening
Insert two gloved fingers in a V beside the nose to hold the vaginal wall off the face
Reposition the mother into knee-chest and wait for the next contraction
quiz.why: The baby is being suffocated by vaginal tissue against the face, so creating an airway is the priority while transporting. Traction can trap the arms above the head and injure the spine, and simply waiting lets the hypoxia continue.

quiz.q: You find a pulsating umbilical cord protruding from the vagina of a laboring patient. What is the priority?
choices: Replace the cord into the vagina gently
Clamp and cut the cord to prevent further prolapse
Position knee-chest and manually lift the presenting part off the cord during transport
Coach the mother to push hard to deliver quickly
quiz.why: Every contraction compresses the cord and cuts fetal oxygen, so relieving pressure and keeping it relieved is the only field intervention. Replacing, clamping or cutting the cord kills the fetus, and pushing increases compression.

quiz.q: A single foot is protruding from the vagina and the mother reports strong contractions. What is the correct management?
choices: Oxygen, knee-chest position, and immediate transport
Gentle traction on the foot with the next contraction
Push the foot back in and await the head
Prepare to deliver on scene as a breech
quiz.why: A limb presentation cannot deliver vaginally in the field and requires a cesarean section. Pulling or replacing the limb causes injury, and it is not a deliverable breech because the body is not presenting.

quiz.q: The newborn's head delivers and retracts tightly against the perineum, and the shoulders will not follow. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Apply fundal pressure at the top of the uterus
Clamp and cut the cord to relieve tension
Rotate the head 180 degrees
Flex the mother's knees sharply toward her chest and apply suprapubic pressure
quiz.why: McRoberts maneuver rotates the pelvis to open the outlet and suprapubic pressure pushes the impacted anterior shoulder under the pubic bone. Fundal pressure drives the shoulder harder into the bone and makes the dystocia worse.

quiz.q: At 1 minute a newborn is pale all over, limp, with a weak irregular gasp, a pulse of 92, and only a faint grimace to stimulation. What is the APGAR score?
quiz.why: Appearance 0 for pallor, Pulse 1 for a rate under 100, Grimace 1 for a faint response, Activity 0 for limp tone, Respirations 1 for a weak irregular effort, totaling 3. That range means full resuscitation.

quiz.q: Which APGAR total is considered normal for a newborn?
choices: 7 to 10
4 to 6
5 to 8
9 to 10 only
quiz.why: A score of 7 to 10 is normal, 4 to 6 is moderately depressed and usually needs stimulation and ventilation, and 0 to 3 needs full resuscitation. Requiring a 9 or 10 would misclassify most healthy newborns with acrocyanosis.

quiz.q: A newborn remains apneic with a heart rate of 74 after drying, warming, positioning and stimulation. What is the next action?
choices: Begin chest compressions at 3 to 1
Give blow-by oxygen and reassess in one minute
Begin positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute
Check a blood glucose level
quiz.why: Apnea or a heart rate under 100 after the initial steps is the trigger for positive-pressure ventilation, which is the highest-yield intervention in newborn resuscitation. Compressions are not indicated until the rate is under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

quiz.q: You have ventilated a newborn effectively for 30 seconds and the heart rate is 48. What now?
choices: Continue ventilation alone and reassess in 2 minutes
Stop ventilation and apply an AED
Start compressions at 15 to 2 with two rescuers
Start compressions using the two-thumb technique at 3 compressions to 1 breath
quiz.why: A rate under 60 after 30 seconds of good ventilation is the threshold for compressions in a newborn, at a 3:1 ratio delivering 120 events per minute. The 15:2 ratio belongs to two-rescuer child and infant CPR, not newborn resuscitation.

quiz.q: Which three components make up the pediatric assessment triangle?
choices: Airway, breathing, circulation
Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure
Tone, temperature, capillary refill
quiz.why: The PAT is a hands-off doorway impression built from appearance, work of breathing and circulation to skin. ABCs come next as a hands-on primary survey, and vital-sign numbers come after that.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old has a normal appearance and normal breathing effort but is mottled with a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a BP of 92/60. What is your impression?
choices: Normal child
Respiratory distress
Compensated shock
Decompensated shock
quiz.why: Only the circulation arm is abnormal, so the child is compensating and still perfusing the brain. The normal blood pressure is expected in compensated shock; if appearance deteriorates, it has become decompensated.

quiz.q: Which respiratory rate would be considered normal for a healthy 6-month-old?
choices: 34 breaths per minute
16 breaths per minute
10 breaths per minute
62 breaths per minute
quiz.why: Infants breathe roughly 25 to 50 times per minute, so 34 is normal. Sixteen would be dangerously slow for an infant, and 62 exceeds the upper limit and suggests distress.

quiz.q: You are ventilating an apneic 4-year-old with a pulse of 110. What rate should you use?
choices: One breath every 6 seconds
Thirty compressions to two breaths
One breath every second
One breath every 2 to 3 seconds
quiz.why: For infants and children with a pulse the current rate is one breath every 2 to 3 seconds, about 20 to 30 per minute. One every 6 seconds is the adult rate and would under-ventilate a child, and 30:2 applies only to arrest with compressions.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old with a fever of 103 F sits forward drooling with a muffled voice and no cough. Which action is contraindicated?
choices: Allowing the child to remain in a position of comfort
Offering blow-by oxygen held by the parent
Inspecting the throat with a tongue blade
Requesting ALS and transporting gently
quiz.why: The picture is epiglottitis, and manipulating the throat can trigger complete laryngospasm and obstruction. Comfort position, blow-by oxygen and a calm gentle transport are all correct; nothing enters the mouth.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old has had a harsh barking cough for two nights, a low-grade fever, and stridor only when crying. What is the most likely condition and the appropriate care?
choices: Croup; keep the child calm with a caregiver, humidified or blow-by oxygen, and transport
Epiglottitis; immediate oral airway placement
Asthma; assist with a metered-dose inhaler
Foreign body; perform abdominal thrusts
quiz.why: A barking cough with gradual onset and stridor only with agitation is croup, and agitation worsens obstruction, so calm plus oxygen and transport is the plan. Epiglottitis has drooling and no cough, and an oral airway in either condition would be harmful.

quiz.q: A 6-week-old has a rectal temperature of 100.8 F and is feeding normally with a happy appearance. What is the correct disposition?
choices: Advise the parents to give fluids and follow up with the pediatrician in the morning
Transport for immediate evaluation because fever under 3 months is an emergency
Cool the infant with a tepid sponge bath and reassess
Transport only if the infant develops a rash
quiz.why: Infants under 3 months cannot localize infection, so a temperature of 100.4 F or higher requires a full hospital work-up regardless of appearance. Waiting for a rash or for worsening behavior misses early sepsis and meningitis.
