quiz.q: A 5-year-old fell from a couch according to the caregiver, but has a curved loop-shaped bruise on the back and several older yellowing bruises on the ears. What should you do?
choices: Confront the caregiver on scene to establish what really happened
Do nothing, since bruising is common in active children
Report only if the child confirms abuse
Document the findings and statements objectively, report to DCP&P, and notify the hospital
quiz.why: Patterned bruises, injuries on protected areas such as the ears, and a mechanism that does not match are abuse red flags, and in New Jersey suspicion alone triggers a mandated report to DCP&P at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. Confronting the caregiver endangers the crew and the child.

quiz.q: An 84-year-old woman with diabetes complains only of sudden shortness of breath, nausea and profound weakness. She denies chest pain. What should you suspect first?
choices: Anxiety attack
Acute coronary syndrome presenting atypically
Simple deconditioning
Medication non-compliance
quiz.why: Age and diabetes both dull pain perception, so a myocardial infarction can present as dyspnea, nausea, weakness or confusion with no chest pain at all. Assuming anxiety or deconditioning in an elderly diabetic is how silent MIs get missed.

quiz.q: A 79-year-old on warfarin struck his head on a cabinet three hours ago. He is alert and oriented with no visible injury. What is the correct approach?
choices: No transport is needed because he is neurologically intact
Transport only if he develops a headache
Have him recheck himself in 24 hours
Transport for evaluation because anticoagulation makes a delayed intracranial bleed likely
quiz.why: Anticoagulants prevent clot formation, so bleeding inside the skull can accumulate slowly and become symptomatic hours later. A normal exam now does not exclude a bleed, and waiting for symptoms wastes the window for reversal.

quiz.q: The family of a patient with a valid DNR asks whether you will still help him breathe comfortably and control his pain. What is the correct response?
choices: A DNR means no treatment of any kind can be provided
A DNR must be honored only after a physician arrives
A DNR means transport is not permitted
A DNR limits resuscitation only; comfort care, oxygen, positioning and transport continue
quiz.why: A DNR or POLST restricts resuscitative measures such as CPR and defibrillation, not supportive care. Withholding oxygen, positioning, comfort measures or transport based on a DNR is a misreading of the document.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 26F, 39 weeks, 'the baby is coming'
scenarios.intro: 0247 hours. Third-floor apartment, no elevator. Dispatch: 26-year-old female, 39 weeks pregnant, third pregnancy, 'feels like she needs to push.' Your partner is carrying the jump bag and the monitor. You have an OB kit in the side compartment. The nearest hospital with obstetrics is 14 minutes away in good traffic.

steps.prompt: The door is open. She is on her hands and knees on the bedroom floor, breathing hard, saying 'it's coming, it's coming.' Her partner is standing in the corner holding a phone. There are towels on the bed.

choices.text: Put on gloves and eye protection, help her onto her back with knees flexed, and look for crowning
choices.feedback: Correct. The single decision that drives everything else is whether she is crowning, and you cannot know without looking. BSI first because delivery is a fluid-heavy event.

choices.text: Get her up and walk her to the stairs for immediate transport
choices.feedback: Dangerous. A third-time mother saying the baby is coming may deliver on a stairwell. Assess for crowning before you decide to move her.

choices.text: Take a full set of vitals and a detailed OB history before examining her
choices.feedback: Too slow. History matters, but with an urge to push in a multipara you look for crowning first and gather history while you set up.

choices.text: Ask her partner how far apart the contractions are and call for ALS before touching her
choices.feedback: Calling for ALS is reasonable, but it does not replace looking. A delivery in progress is time-critical and only your eyes can confirm it.

steps.prompt: You get her onto her back with knees flexed and hips propped on a folded blanket. The top of the baby's head is visible at the vaginal opening and does not recede between contractions. Contractions are about 2 minutes apart and last roughly 80 seconds.

choices.text: Open the OB kit, drape her, and prepare to deliver here
choices.feedback: Right call. Crowning plus contractions 2 minutes apart lasting 60 to 90 seconds in a third pregnancy is an on-scene delivery. Bring the whole kit to her side now.

choices.text: Carry her down three flights in a stair chair and deliver in the ambulance
choices.feedback: No. You would be moving a crowning patient down a stairwell. Delivering on a controlled scene with light and space is far safer than a moving compartment.

choices.text: Tell her to pant and not push so you can get her to the hospital
choices.feedback: Panting between pushes helps control the head, but you cannot stop this delivery. Set up to catch the baby, not to stall it.

steps.prompt: With the next contraction the head delivers face-down and then rotates to the side. You feel around the neck and find the umbilical cord wrapped once, and it is loose enough to move.

choices.text: Gently slip the cord over the baby's head
choices.feedback: Correct. A loose nuchal cord is slipped over the head so the baby keeps its oxygen supply through the placenta until delivery is complete.

choices.text: Clamp the cord twice and cut between the clamps right away
choices.feedback: Unnecessary and harmful here. Cutting the cord ends the baby's oxygen supply, so it is reserved for a cord too tight to slip, followed by immediate delivery.

choices.text: Pull the baby out quickly by the head to beat the next contraction
choices.feedback: Never pull on the head. Traction injures the neck and brachial nerves, and it does not fix a nuchal cord.

choices.text: Suction the mouth and nose thoroughly before doing anything else
choices.feedback: Routine suctioning is no longer recommended, and it delays dealing with the cord around the neck, which is the actual threat right now.

steps.prompt: You guide the head gently downward and the top shoulder delivers, then gently upward and the rest of the baby slides out at 0301. The infant is blue, limp, and not crying. There is no meconium.

choices.text: Dry vigorously, discard the wet towel, wrap including the head, position the airway neutral, and rub the back
choices.feedback: Exactly. Warm, dry, stimulate and position is the first 30 seconds for every newborn, and it alone revives most depressed babies.

choices.text: Begin chest compressions immediately
choices.feedback: Far too early. You have not dried, stimulated or checked a heart rate. Newborn compressions come only after 30 seconds of effective ventilation with a rate under 60.

choices.text: Deep-suction the airway with a catheter to clear the lungs
choices.feedback: Not indicated with clear fluid, and deep suctioning can cause reflex bradycardia. Wipe the face, dry and stimulate instead.

choices.text: Clamp and cut the cord first so you can move the baby to the bench seat
choices.feedback: Understandable but out of order. Dry, warm and stimulate where the baby is; you can work at the mother's side, and early clamping is reserved for a baby needing resuscitation.

steps.prompt: After 30 seconds of drying and stimulation the baby takes a few weak gasps then stops. You feel the base of the cord: 8 beats in 6 seconds. Skin is still dusky centrally.

choices.text: Begin positive-pressure ventilation with an infant BVM at 40 to 60 breaths per minute, just enough for chest rise
choices.feedback: Correct. Apnea or a heart rate under 100 means ventilate. This is the single highest-yield action in newborn resuscitation, and this baby is at 80.

choices.text: Start chest compressions at 3 to 1 with ventilations
choices.feedback: Premature. Compressions are added only when the rate stays under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation. At 80 with no breathing, ventilation is the treatment.

choices.text: Hold oxygen tubing near the face and continue rubbing the back
choices.feedback: Blow-by oxygen does nothing for a baby who is not breathing. Stimulation has already failed; the baby needs air moved for it.

choices.text: Clamp and cut the cord now, then ventilate
choices.feedback: Acceptable sequence — a newborn needing resuscitation is separated early rather than waiting 1 to 3 minutes — but do not let it delay the first breaths by more than a few seconds.

steps.prompt: After 30 seconds of ventilation with visible chest rise, the heart rate is 136 and the baby begins crying and pinking up. The mother is still on the floor with the cord clamped and the placenta undelivered. Estimated blood loss so far is moderate.

choices.text: Stop ventilating, keep the baby dry and warm skin-to-skin with mom, score the 5-minute APGAR, massage the fundus, and package both for transport
choices.feedback: Correct on every count. Rate over 100 with spontaneous breathing means stop PPV. Warmth, the 5-minute APGAR, fundal massage and transport together are the full package.

choices.text: Continue bagging at 40 to 60 per minute until arrival at the hospital
choices.feedback: Over-treatment. Once the heart rate is over 100 and the baby is breathing on its own, ventilation stops. Continued bagging risks lung injury and gastric distension.

choices.text: Wait on scene for the placenta before transporting, and apply gentle cord traction to speed it up
choices.feedback: Two errors. You never delay transport for the placenta, and cord traction can invert the uterus and cause massive hemorrhage.

choices.text: Wrap the baby and set it on the bench seat alone while you finish care for the mother
choices.feedback: Unsafe. An unsecured newborn on a bench seat can fall, and separating them loses the heat transfer of skin-to-skin contact. Secure the infant properly.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: crowning decides the location, and everything after that is warmth and airway. You confirmed imminent delivery with your eyes, delivered on scene because a multipara at 2-minute contractions will not wait, managed the nuchal cord without cutting it, and then treated a depressed newborn in the correct order — dry, warm, stimulate, position, then ventilate at 40 to 60 when the heart rate was under 100, and stop when it rose over 100. Compressions never entered the picture because ventilation worked, which is true of almost every newborn resuscitation. Two things kill babies on these calls: cold and no air moving. You fixed both.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 2-year-old, fever and trouble breathing
scenarios.intro: 2210 hours. Single-family home. Dispatch: 2-year-old male, fever and 'a weird cough, having trouble breathing.' Mother meets you at the door and says he has been sick for two days and it got much worse tonight. Your bag has pediatric BVMs, a nonrebreather, a nasal cannula, a pulse oximeter and a glucometer.

steps.prompt: You stop in the doorway of the living room before touching anything. What is your first assessment?

choices.text: Form a pediatric assessment triangle from the doorway: appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
choices.feedback: Correct. The PAT takes about six seconds, requires no hands, and tells you sick or not sick before you upset the child. Touching first makes a child cry and hides everything.

choices.text: Walk over, pick the child up, and attach a pulse oximeter
choices.feedback: You just lost your best data. Separating a sick toddler from a parent and applying equipment causes crying, which changes respiratory effort, color and heart rate.

choices.text: Take a full history from the mother before looking at the child
choices.feedback: History matters but comes second. Look at the child first; if the PAT is grossly abnormal, you act before the story is finished.

steps.prompt: Appearance: awake, tired-looking, tracks you with his eyes, reaches for his mother and settles when she holds him. Work of breathing: mild retractions between the ribs, a harsh seal-like barking cough, and a high-pitched noise on breathing in when he gets upset. Circulation to skin: pink cheeks, no mottling, no cyanosis.

choices.text: Impression: respiratory distress from an upper-airway obstruction, most consistent with croup
choices.feedback: Correct. Abnormal work of breathing with a normal appearance and normal skin equals distress, not failure. A barking cough with stridor only on agitation is the croup pattern.

choices.text: Impression: respiratory failure requiring immediate bag-valve-mask ventilation
choices.feedback: Over-call. Appearance is normal and he is consolable, which means the brain is being perfused and oxygenated. Failure requires an abnormal appearance.

choices.text: Impression: epiglottitis, so avoid all airway assessment
choices.feedback: Wrong pattern, right instinct about the throat. Epiglottitis brings drooling, a tripod posture, a muffled voice and no cough. A barking cough points away from it.

choices.text: Impression: compensated shock from dehydration
choices.feedback: The circulation arm is normal — pink, no mottling, good consolability — so shock is not the lead problem, though two days of fever means you should still ask about fluids and wet diapers.

steps.prompt: The mother asks what you are going to do. The child is clinging to her, quiet as long as nobody approaches with equipment. Stridor returns every time he startles.

choices.text: Leave him in his mother's arms, have her hold blow-by oxygen near his face, keep the room calm, and prepare for gentle transport
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Agitation increases turbulent flow through a narrowed airway and worsens obstruction. A calm child on a parent's lap moves more air than a fighting child with a perfect mask seal.

choices.text: Open his mouth with a tongue depressor to inspect the throat and confirm the diagnosis
choices.feedback: Never. You do not manipulate the throat of a child with stridor. If you were wrong and this is epiglottitis, that maneuver can cause complete obstruction.

choices.text: Strap a pediatric nonrebreather tightly to his face and lay him supine on the stretcher
choices.feedback: Both halves are wrong. Forcing a mask causes screaming, and lying a child with upper-airway swelling flat worsens the obstruction. Let him sit up with a parent.

choices.text: Insert an oropharyngeal airway to keep the airway open during transport
choices.feedback: He is awake with a gag reflex, so an OPA is contraindicated and would trigger vomiting and laryngospasm. The obstruction is below where an OPA reaches anyway.

steps.prompt: Consider a different child at the same address next week: a 4-year-old, high fever, sitting bolt upright leaning forward on her hands, drooling onto her shirt, a muffled voice, and no cough at all. She looks frightened and ill.

choices.text: Suspect epiglottitis: nothing in the mouth, let her choose her own position, blow-by oxygen, calm quiet transport, request ALS
choices.feedback: Correct. Drooling, tripod posture, muffled voice, high fever and no cough is epiglottitis. The airway is one spasm from closing, so you do nothing that provokes her.

choices.text: Lay her flat, suction the drool, and inspect the airway
choices.feedback: Any one of those three could kill her. Supine position, suctioning the pharynx and visualizing the throat all risk triggering complete obstruction.

choices.text: Assist with the family's albuterol inhaler for the noisy breathing
choices.feedback: Albuterol works on the lower airways. Epiglottic swelling is above the cords, so it does nothing here and the delay costs you time.

choices.text: Have her lie on her side and start an IV line for antibiotics
choices.feedback: IV access and antibiotics are out of EMT scope, and any procedure that upsets her increases obstruction risk. Position of comfort and gentle transport are the field treatment.

steps.prompt: Back to the 2-year-old with croup. He is loaded on the stretcher in his mother's lap, secured, with blow-by oxygen. Halfway to the hospital he becomes quieter, the retractions deepen, and the stridor is now audible at rest even when he is not upset.

choices.text: Recognize deterioration toward respiratory failure: notify the hospital, request an ALS intercept, and be ready to assist ventilation with a pediatric BVM
choices.feedback: Correct. Stridor at rest, deepening retractions, falling saturation and a quieter child mean the appearance arm is now abnormal. That is failure, and it demands escalation.

choices.text: Take it as improvement, since he is calmer and making less noise
choices.feedback: A dangerous misread. Getting quiet while working harder is exhaustion, not recovery, and it precedes arrest in children.

choices.text: Increase oxygen flow and continue without notifying anyone
choices.feedback: Oxygen is appropriate but insufficient on its own. Failing to notify the hospital or call for ALS wastes the time you have left.

choices.text: Pull over and attempt to intubate
choices.feedback: Out of EMT scope and the wrong instinct for a swollen upper airway. Bag-valve-mask ventilation with a good seal is the EMT-level rescue, with ALS en route.

scenarios.debrief: Two lessons stacked here. First, the PAT works from the doorway: appearance abnormal means the brain is in trouble, breathing abnormal means the lungs or airway, skin abnormal means perfusion. This child started with only one abnormal arm — distress — and ended with two, which is failure. Second, upper-airway obstruction is a calm-versus-crying problem. Croup barks and gets loud when upset; epiglottitis drools, tripods, and has no cough at all. For either one, nothing goes in the mouth, the child stays in whatever position they chose, and a parent holds the oxygen. The single most important sign to carry out of this case: a child who stops fighting and gets quiet while their work of breathing rises is not improving — they are running out.
